The Great potoo (Nyctibius grandis) is a large, nocturnal neotropical bird known for its remarkable cryptic plumage, which allows it to perch motionless on broken branches, effectively resembling a stump. Before hatching, the fertilised egg is incubated for an extended period; eggs that are artificially incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] produce healthy chicks after approximately 30 days [ab = approximately 30 days]. This incubation duration, measured in captive rearing programs, yields a neonate that emerges from the calcareous egg after a substantially longer developmental period than those of related caprimulgiforms of comparable egg mass. Upon emergence, the initial egg weight of the species has been reported at roughly 42 grams [Ww0 = roughly 42 grams], a value that is typical for a bird with an adult body mass that approaches the upper end of the potoo size range. The nesting adult, which typically lays a single white egg in a natural tree cavity, exhibits strong site fidelity, and the parents share incubation duties during the roughly 30-day post-oviposition period.

Under the thermal conditions associated with active metabolic periods in controlled environments (40 °C [T = 40 °C]), the altricial nestling undergoes a significant growth spurt during its first weeks after hatching. By the time the developing chick reaches five weeks since birth, it attains a weight of 162 grams  at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This value, based on approximately two-thirds of adult length at five weeks, indicates that the young individual accumulates mass rapidly during the early nestling phase, a period dominated by parental provisioning. The pre-recessive juvenile grows from a downy chick into a feather-growing nestling, progressively developing the distinctive barred plumage. Ultimately, the growing bird will achieve an ultimate wet weight of 546 grams [Wwi = 546 grams] as a sexually mature adult, a body size that makes it the largest species within its genus. Field records suggest that this asymptotic mass is generally stable across its range from southern Mexico through to Bolivia.

The fledgling independence phase occurs relatively early in this species when considered alongside its large body size. Under the thermal condition of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], a typical immature bird achieves its first flight and completes nest departure after about 60 days since birth [tx = about 60 days since birth]. This transition marks the end of direct parental provisioning cessation, though the fledgling may remain within the natal territory for several additional weeks, slowly acquiring foraging skills through observational learning. The achievement of first flight represents a critical developmental milestone, enabling the young bird to escape terrestrial predators and to begin dispersing to suitable habitat patches. After leaving the nest, the juvenile bird gradually develops the hunting proficiency required to capture large insects and small vertebrates on the wing during nocturnal forays. This period of post-fledging dispersal is a time of elevated mortality risk, with young individuals often falling prey to larger raptors or snakes before establishing their own territories.

A key life-history transition for Nyctibius grandis is the attainment of puberty, which occurs under a stable temperature regime of 40 °C [T = 40 °C] after approximately 180 days since birth [tp = approximately 180 days since birth]. This marks the beginning of gonadal activation and the onset of reproductive maturity, although most individuals delay actual breeding until they have secured a permanent territory. The time since birth at first brood is considerably later, as the species defers its first successful reproduction to roughly 640 days since birth [tR = roughly 640 days since birth] under these same thermal conditions at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This extended pre-breeding interval is characteristic of a relatively slow life-history pace, consistent with the pattern observed in other large-bodied, long-lived caprimulgiforms. During this period, the young adult continues to refine its hunting skills and strengthens its pair bond with a mate, often reusing the same nesting site in successive years. Field observations indicate that first breeding attempts can sometimes be postponed further if competition for high-quality nesting cavities is intense.

The maximum recorded longevity for Nyctibius grandis is estimated at 40 years [am = 40 years] when measured under controlled conditions at 40 °C [T = 40 °C], a value that positions this species among the longest-lived members of the Caprimulgiformes, likely as a consequence of its low adult mortality rate afforded by exceptional cryptic coloration. As the breeding adult bird ages, female reproductive output remains relatively stable for many years before a gradual decline associated with reproductive senescence. The species deposits a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch] and typically produces one clutch each year [F_R_i = one clutch each year], an exceptionally low annual reproductive output among birds that reflects a strategy prioritizing high parental investment in a single offspring. The senescent adult ultimately succumbs to natural mortality after completing its lifespan, leaving behind a complex population structure that depends critically on high adult survival rates to maintain stable numbers.
